promises.quote: Each response includes a monotonically increasing `sequence_number`, which allows you to track when this request is actually persisted to the Raft log.
promises.plain: Every queued-write response on a given node carries a sequence number strictly greater than any earlier one from that node.
promises.when_to_inject: Between two queued writes, step the host wall clock backwards by several seconds or minutes. Repeat the check across a kill -9 and restart of the node.
promises.outside_observation: Record every sequence_number Fuss receives from the node, in send order, in Fuss's own history file. Any value less than or equal to an earlier value from the same node breaks the promise.
promises.workload_sketch: Loop: POST /db/execute?queue with one INSERT, then log sequence_number. Mid-loop, set the clock back 10 minutes. Continue. Then kill -9 rqlited, restart it with the same flags and data dir, and continue the loop.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the example values look like nanosecond wall-clock timestamps. If the counter is seeded from wall time, a backwards clock step or a restart after a step could produce smaller numbers.

promises.quote: The `/status` [diagnostics](/docs/guides/monitoring-rqlite) endpoint includes the sequence number of the latest request successfully written to Raft.
promises.plain: Once /status reports a sequence number at least as large as a request's sequence number, that request is in the Raft log and survives a crash.
promises.when_to_inject: Immediately after /status first reports a persisted sequence number greater than or equal to a given write's sequence_number.
promises.outside_observation: After restart, run a strong-consistency query for the rows of every write whose sequence number /status had reported as persisted before the kill. Each such row must be present.
promises.workload_sketch: Start rqlited with a large -write-queue-capacity/batch size and a timeout of a few seconds. POST /db/execute?queue with uniquely tagged INSERTs. Poll GET /status until the queue's reported sequence number is at least the write's number. Kill -9. Restart. GET /db/query?level=strong SELECT tags.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the status counter might be updated when the batch is handed to Raft rather than after the commit is durable, so a kill in that window loses data the counter claimed was written.

promises.quote: You can explicitly tell the request to wait until the queue has persisted all pending requests.
promises.plain: A queued write sent with `wait` that returns success means it, and every request queued before it, has been persisted.
promises.when_to_inject: Right after a successful response to a `?queue&wait` request is received.
promises.outside_observation: After restart, all rows from that request and from every earlier acknowledged queued request on the same node must be present.
promises.workload_sketch: POST several ?queue INSERTs (no wait), then POST ?queue&wait&timeout=10s with one INSERT. On 200, kill -9 immediately. Restart. SELECT with level=strong and check every row is present.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: `wait` might only cover the batch containing this request, not all earlier pending batches, or it might return before the fsync.

promises.quote: If the queue has not emptied after this time, the request will return with an error. If not set, the timeout is 30 seconds.
promises.plain: If the queue cannot be flushed in time, a `wait` request returns an error rather than success, and the default limit is 30 seconds.
promises.when_to_inject: Fill the data directory's filesystem before sending the `?queue&wait` request. In a cluster variant, kill the leader instead.
promises.outside_observation: The response must be an error, not 200, and must arrive at about the given timeout (or about 30 seconds when no timeout is set). It must never be success without the data being readable later.
promises.workload_sketch: Fill the disk with a loop-mounted small filesystem. POST /db/execute?queue&wait&timeout=3s INSERT and time the response. Repeat without the timeout parameter and expect about 30 seconds.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a write error inside the background flush might be swallowed. That could empty the queue (counted as done) and report success, or hang past the timeout.

promises.quote: The net result is as if the client wrote a single Bulk request containing all the queued statements.
promises.plain: Queued statements are applied in the order they were queued, just as if they had been sent as one bulk request.
promises.when_to_inject: During heavy sequential queuing from one client, while other clients also queue writes. Optionally add a restart between batches.
promises.outside_observation: Use statements whose result depends on order, for example UPDATE x SET v=v*2 and UPDATE x SET v=v+1. Also use INSERTs into an AUTOINCREMENT table. Compare the final state and rowid order with the order in Fuss's own send log, which follows sequence_number order.
promises.workload_sketch: Client A sends a serial chain of ?queue requests, each awaiting its response before the next: INSERT tag=i. Clients B and C run concurrently. After a final ?queue&wait, SELECT id,tag ORDER BY id and check that A's tags increase.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: retries or batch merging under load could reorder a retried batch after a later one.

promises.quote: there is a small risk of data loss in the event the node crashes before queued data is persisted. You can make this window arbitrarily small by adjusting the queuing parameters, at the cost of write performance.
promises.plain: A crash can lose only queued data that was not yet persisted. Shrinking the batch size and timeout shrinks the set of writes at risk.
promises.when_to_inject: At random moments during a steady stream of queued writes, run once with a small batch size and timeout and once with large settings.
promises.outside_observation: After restart, the lost writes must be a suffix of the acknowledged writes: all with sequence numbers above the last persisted value. The count lost should be bounded by about the batch size or the writes sent within one timeout. No earlier write should be missing (no gaps).
promises.workload_sketch: rqlited -write-queue-capacity/-write-queue-batch-size=1 -write-queue-timeout=10ms. Stream ?queue INSERTs. Kill -9 at a random time. Restart. Diff the acknowledged rows against the stored rows. Repeat with batch size 1000 and timeout 5s.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: if batches are flushed concurrently, a later batch could commit while an earlier one is lost, leaving a gap rather than a lost suffix.

promises.quote: By default, a node will retry a Queued Write once if the Leader is not reachable. This does mean that if a Queued Write appeared to fail, but was actually successful (the response from the Leader may be dropped by the network), data may be duplicated. You can eliminate this risk by setting `-write-queue-retry` to zero.
promises.plain: With -write-queue-retry=0, each queued write is applied at most once. With the default, it is retried at most once, so it can appear at most twice.
promises.when_to_inject: In a 3-node cluster, send queued writes to a follower and kill -9 or SIGSTOP the leader while the follower is forwarding a batch.
promises.outside_observation: Use uniquely tagged INSERTs into a table without a UNIQUE constraint and count each tag. With retry=0, any tag count above 1 breaks the promise. With the default, any count above 2 breaks it.
promises.workload_sketch: Start 3 nodes with -write-queue-retry=0. POST follower:/db/execute?queue INSERT tag=uuid in a loop. Kill or pause the leader repeatedly. After the cluster recovers, run SELECT tag,count(*) GROUP BY tag HAVING count(*)>1.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the forwarding client or the Raft layer might retry independently of the -write-queue-retry setting, causing duplicates even at zero.

promises.quote: By default, writes from the queue are not performed within a transaction. If you wish to change this, it must be set at launch time via the command-line option `-write-queue-tx`.
promises.plain: With -write-queue-tx, each queued batch is applied atomically, all or nothing. Without it, statements are applied independently.
promises.when_to_inject: Queue a batch that contains one statement that will fail (a constraint violation) among valid ones. Optionally also kill -9 during the flush.
promises.outside_observation: With -write-queue-tx, the batch must apply all of its rows or none, and none if one statement fails. Without it, valid rows appear even though one statement failed. After a kill, there must never be a partial batch under -write-queue-tx.
promises.workload_sketch: Start rqlited -write-queue-tx with a large batch size. Within one timeout window, POST ?queue INSERT a, ?queue INSERT duplicate-primary-key, ?queue INSERT b, then ?queue&wait. SELECT and check that a and b are both absent or both present, consistent with the transaction. Repeat without -write-queue-tx.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the transaction might wrap each original request instead of the merged batch, making atomicity per request rather than per batch.

promises.quote: rqlite merges queued requests when the configured batch size is reached or a configurable timeout expires. It then executes them as a single request.
promises.plain: A partly filled queue is still flushed once the configured timeout expires, even if the batch size is never reached.
promises.when_to_inject: Right after queuing a single request with a huge batch size, step the wall clock forward or backward.
promises.outside_observation: The row becomes visible to a strong read, and /status's persisted sequence number advances, within about the configured timeout. It is neither delayed indefinitely nor flushed early because of the clock jump.
promises.workload_sketch: Start rqlited with batch size 100000 and -write-queue-timeout=2s. POST one ?queue INSERT. Set the clock back 1 hour. Poll GET /db/query?level=strong until the row appears, and measure elapsed time with Fuss's own monotonic clock.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: if the flush timer relies on wall-clock deadlines instead of a monotonic timer, a backwards step could stall the flush.

promises.quote: This type of read is, as the name suggests, linearizable: such reads reflect a state of the system at some point after the read was initiated, and each read will at least return the results of the latest committed write[^1].
promises.plain: A read with level=linearizable must reflect every write that was acknowledged before the read started, so the read history is linearizable.
promises.when_to_inject: Repeatedly SIGKILL the current Leader (found via /status) while concurrent writes and linearizable reads are in flight, then restart it with the same flags.
promises.outside_observation: Fuss logs the invoke and complete times of each operation and the value returned. A linearizability checker (Porcupine-style) on a register or counter model must accept the history. A read that completes successfully but misses a write acknowledged before the read started is a violation. Errors and timeouts are treated as indeterminate.
promises.workload_sketch: Start a 3-node cluster. CREATE TABLE r(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, v INTEGER). Run N clients. Each client randomly either POSTs /db/execute 'UPDATE r SET v=? WHERE id=1' with unique values, or GETs /db/query?level=linearizable 'SELECT v FROM r WHERE id=1', sending requests to random nodes. Kill and restart the Leader every few seconds.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a deposed Leader could record the commit index or pass the heartbeat quorum check before learning it was deposed. Or it could read before the entry at the recorded commit index is applied to SQLite after a restart replay.

promises.quote: Finally -- and this is critical -- the Leader waits until the write request at the previously recorded commit index has been applied to the SQLite database. Once this happens it then performs the read.
promises.plain: A linearizable read must never return data older than the commit index that existed when the read arrived, even right after a restart or leader change.
promises.when_to_inject: Restart a node, or kill the Leader so another node takes over. Then immediately issue linearizable reads while the new Leader is still replaying its log into SQLite.
promises.outside_observation: Every successful read returns a value at least as new as the last write acknowledged before the read was sent. The value is identified by a monotonic sequence number that Fuss writes.
promises.workload_sketch: Write seq=1..K with acknowledgements. Kill the Leader. As soon as /status shows a new Leader, loop GET /db/query?level=linearizable 'SELECT max(seq) FROM t' and check that the result is >= K.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: after a leader change, the applied index on the new Leader may lag its commit index, and the wait-for-apply step could race with log replay.

promises.quote: _Strong_ reads accomplish this by sending the query through the actual Raft log. This will, of course, involve the Leader contacting at least a quorum of nodes, some disk I/O, and will therefore increase query response times. _Strong_ reads are linearizable.
promises.plain: Reads with level=strong are linearizable and reflect all committed writes.
promises.when_to_inject: During concurrent writes and strong reads, kill the Leader or a quorum-member follower, then restart it.
promises.outside_observation: A linearizability checker over Fuss's recorded history accepts all successful strong reads. No successful strong read misses a previously acknowledged write.
promises.workload_sketch: Same register workload as the linearizable test, but use GET /db/query?level=strong. Send some reads to followers to exercise forwarding.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a strong read entry committed just as leadership changes could be answered from a node whose SQLite is not yet caught up.

promises.quote: Specifically when you use _Strong_ all currently committed entries in the Raft log have also been applied to the SQLite database at the time the read request is executed.
promises.plain: A successful strong read sees every write committed before it.
promises.when_to_inject: Fill the Leader's data-directory filesystem while strong reads and writes are running. Strong reads write to the Raft log.
promises.outside_observation: Strong reads either return an error or return data that includes all acknowledged writes. A success that misses an acknowledged write is a violation.
promises.workload_sketch: Ack writes seq=1..K. Fill the Leader's disk. Loop GET /db/query?level=strong 'SELECT max(seq) FROM t'. Free the disk and repeat.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: if the log append for the read fails on ENOSPC, an error path might fall back to a local read instead of returning an error.

promises.quote: If the node determines it is not the Leader, the node will transparently forward the request to the Leader, which will in turn perform a _Weak_ read of its database. In that case the node waits for the response from the Leader, and then returns that response to the client.
promises.plain: A weak read sent to a follower returns the Leader's data, not the follower's local data.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill and restart followers, but not the Leader, so that a restarted follower's local SQLite lags behind. Then read from that follower.
promises.outside_observation: While the Leader is stable, a weak read sent to the lagging follower returns the latest acknowledged value from the Leader. Fuss can confirm the follower is lagging with level=none on the same follower.
promises.workload_sketch: Kill follower F. Write seq=1..K via the Leader. Restart F. Immediately GET F:/db/query?level=weak and F:/db/query?level=none. The weak read should show K even when the none read shows less.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a freshly restarted follower might briefly think it is Leader, or might serve locally before it learns who the Leader is.

promises.quote: However there is a small window of time (less than a second by default) during which a node may think it's the Leader, but has actually been deposed, a new Leader elected, and other writes have taken place on the cluster.
promises.plain: Stale weak reads can only happen within less than about one second after a leader is deposed.
promises.when_to_inject: Pause or kill-restart the Leader in ways that cause a leader change while writes keep going to the new Leader.
promises.outside_observation: Fuss checks every stale weak read. A stale read is one that misses a write acknowledged more than about 1s, plus timing slack, before the read was invoked. A stale read outside that window is a violation.
promises.workload_sketch: Run the register workload with weak reads sent to all nodes. Use SIGSTOP/SIGCONT on the Leader for a few seconds to force deposition, then let it resume and keep serving. Measure how old each stale read is.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a node resumed after a long pause may still believe it is Leader until its own lease or heartbeat timer fires, which could exceed one second.

promises.quote: _Weak_ consistency is used if you don't specify any level, or if an unrecognized level is specified
promises.plain: A query with no level, or an unknown level, behaves exactly like level=weak.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill a quorum so that no Leader exists, and also test with a stable Leader.
promises.outside_observation: With a stable Leader, level=bogus sent to a follower returns the Leader's data, just like weak. With no Leader, it errors like weak and does not silently serve local data like none.
promises.workload_sketch: Send GET /db/query?level=bogus and GET /db/query with no level to a lagging follower and compare against level=weak and level=none. Then kill 2 of 3 nodes and repeat on the survivor.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: parameter parsing could map unknown values to a zero value that corresponds to none.

promises.quote: _None_ consistency is required if a node restarts and, for whatever reason, can't contact the cluster Leader. Using _None_ will instruct the node to query the database as it finds it after restarting. If you select any other consistency level the node will return an error.
promises.plain: A restarted node that cannot reach a Leader serves level=none from local data and returns errors for every other level.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill all nodes, then restart only one node of a 3-node cluster so it cannot reach a Leader.
promises.outside_observation: level=none succeeds. Its data contains only values that some client actually wrote, and it reflects a prefix of the acknowledged history. weak, linearizable, strong, and auto (on a voter) return errors rather than results.
promises.workload_sketch: Ack writes seq=1..K. Kill all nodes. Start one node with its original flags. Query level=none, weak, linearizable, strong, and auto.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the restarted node might hang on non-none levels instead of returning an error, or might serve weak locally if it has stale Leader state persisted.

promises.quote: If a read request sets the query parameter `freshness` to a [Go duration string](https://golang.org/pkg/time/#Duration), the node serving the read will check that less time has passed since it was last in contact with the Leader, than that specified via freshness. If more time has passed the node will return an error.
promises.plain: level=none with freshness=D must return an error once the follower has been out of contact with the Leader for longer than D.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the Leader and enough nodes that no new Leader can be elected. Then wait longer than D before querying the surviving follower.
promises.outside_observation: Fuss knows the kill time. Reads with freshness=1s issued more than 1s plus slack after the kill must error. Reads issued well before that may succeed.
promises.workload_sketch: Start a 3-node cluster. Kill 2 nodes including the Leader. Poll the survivor with GET /db/query?level=none&freshness=1s every 100ms for 5s and record which reads succeed and which error.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: last-contact time might be updated by events other than Leader contact, such as a failed vote request, so the node keeps appearing fresh.

promises.quote: If a read request sets the query parameter `freshness` to a [Go duration string](https://golang.org/pkg/time/#Duration), the node serving the read will check that less time has passed since it was last in contact with the Leader, than that specified via freshness.
promises.plain: The freshness check should not be fooled by wall-clock jumps on the follower.
promises.when_to_inject: After isolating a follower (Leader killed, no quorum), step the follower's wall clock backward by several seconds.
promises.outside_observation: Reads with freshness=1s must still error once real elapsed time exceeds 1s. Success after a backward clock step would show reliance on wall time.
promises.workload_sketch: Kill 2 of 3 nodes. Step the survivor's clock back by 10s. Poll GET /db/query?level=none&freshness=1s for 5s.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: last-contact may be compared using wall-clock time.Now without monotonic readings if the timestamp is serialized or reconstructed.

promises.quote: **The `freshness` parameter is always ignored if the node serving the query is the Leader**. Any read, when served by the Leader, is always going to be within any possible freshness bound. `freshness` is also ignored for all consistency levels except `none`, and is also ignored if set to zero.
promises.plain: freshness never causes an error on the Leader, at levels other than none, or when set to zero.
promises.when_to_inject: Right after a Leader restarts and is re-elected. Also on an isolated follower when testing freshness=0.
promises.outside_observation: GET on the Leader with level=none&freshness=1ns succeeds. Weak or linearizable reads with a tiny freshness behave as if freshness were absent. level=none&freshness=0s on an isolated follower succeeds even after a long disconnection.
promises.workload_sketch: Query the Leader with level=none&freshness=1ns. Query a follower with level=weak&freshness=1ns. Kill 2 of 3 nodes, wait 5s, and query the survivor with level=none&freshness=0s.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a newly elected Leader may not have initialized its last-contact field and could apply the freshness check to itself.

promises.quote: If you also want the node to check that the data it last **applied** to the database is not out-of-date by (at most) the `freshness` interval, you should also add the `freshness_strict` flag as a query parameter.
promises.plain: With freshness_strict, a follower errors unless its last applied entry was appended by the Leader within the freshness interval.
promises.when_to_inject: Restart a follower while writes continue on the Leader, so the follower is in contact but behind on applying entries.
promises.outside_observation: Fuss compares results with and without freshness_strict. A strict read that succeeds must not miss writes acknowledged more than the freshness interval, plus slack, before the read. Fuss assumes clocks are synchronized for this test.
promises.workload_sketch: Write timestamped rows continuously at about 10/s. Kill a follower, wait 5s, and restart it. Immediately poll it with level=none&freshness=1s&freshness_strict and with level=none&freshness=1s. Compare max(ts) in each result with Fuss's write log.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: after restart, the follower might use the timestamp of an older replayed entry or of a heartbeat rather than of the last applied data entry.

promises.quote: **Note that this check works by comparing timestamps generated by the Leader to those generated by the node receiving the read request**. Any clock skew between the nodes may therefore affect the correctness of the data returned by the node.
promises.plain: freshness_strict correctness depends on clock sync, so skew changes results in a predictable direction.
promises.when_to_inject: Skew the follower's clock behind the Leader's by more than the freshness interval while the follower is lagging.
promises.outside_observation: Fuss documents that a follower clock behind the Leader lets stale strict reads succeed and a follower clock ahead causes spurious errors. This characterizes the documented risk rather than a hard violation.
promises.workload_sketch: Pause a follower with SIGSTOP to make it lag. Set its clock -5s, resume it, and query level=none&freshness=1s&freshness_strict. Repeat with +5s.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: this is documented as user responsibility, so failures here are expected. Fuss is only checking that the direction matches the doc.

promises.quote: In the case of a read replica _None_ is chosen as the level. In all other cases _Weak_ is chosen as the level.
promises.plain: level=auto acts as none (honoring freshness) on read replicas and as weak (ignoring freshness) on voting nodes.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill all voting nodes so neither the replica nor any voter can reach a Leader.
promises.outside_observation: On a replica started with -raft-non-voter=true, auto&freshness=1s succeeds shortly after the kill and errors after more than 1s. On a voter with no Leader, auto errors regardless of freshness, matching weak.
promises.workload_sketch: Start 3 voters and 1 non-voter replica. Write data. Kill the voters. Poll the replica with GET /db/query?level=auto&freshness=1s over time. Restart one voter alone and query it with level=auto&freshness=1h.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a replica's role detection could depend on cluster state that is unavailable when the Leader is gone, causing auto to fall back to weak.

promises.quote: If you set a read consistency level other than _None_ when querying a read replica then the replica will simply forward the request to the Leader (which negates the read-scaling benefits of the replica).
promises.plain: A read replica forwards non-none reads to the Leader and returns the Leader's data.
promises.when_to_inject: Restart the replica so that it is lagging, while writes continue.
promises.outside_observation: level=weak on the lagging replica returns the latest acknowledged write, while level=none on the same replica may return older data.
promises.workload_sketch: Kill the replica. Write seq=1..K. Restart the replica and immediately query it with level=weak and level=none for max(seq).
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a replica that has not yet learned the Leader address after restart may error or serve locally.

promises.quote: If a linearizable read is not available within 1 second of receiving the read request, an error will be returned.
promises.plain: With linearizable_timeout=1s, a linearizable read that cannot complete returns an error within about 1 second instead of hanging or returning stale data.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill all followers so the Leader cannot obtain a heartbeat quorum, then issue the read.
promises.outside_observation: Fuss measures latency. The response is an error that arrives within 1s plus slack. A successful result, or a hang well beyond the timeout, is a violation.
promises.workload_sketch: Start a 3-node cluster. Kill both followers. GET Leader:/db/query?level=linearizable&linearizable_timeout=1s 'SELECT 1' and time it.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the timeout may cover only the heartbeat wait and not the wait-for-apply phase, or it may not start until after the forwarding hop.

promises.quote: The read request will be served by the node if it is the Leader, and if it remained the Leader throughout the processing of the read.
promises.plain: A linearizable or strong read must not succeed if the serving node lost leadership mid-read.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the followers, or SIGSTOP the Leader and resume it after a new election, while linearizable reads are in flight on the old Leader.
promises.outside_observation: No successful read from the old Leader returns data missing writes that the new Leader acknowledged before the read completed. Fuss checks this with the linearizability checker.
promises.workload_sketch: Issue a stream of linearizable reads to Leader L. SIGSTOP L for 3s while writes go to the new Leader, then SIGCONT L. Check the reads that L completed after resuming.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the quorum heartbeat responses may have been collected before the pause and still be counted after it.

promises.quote: If an rqlite process crashes, it is safe to simply restart it. The node will pick up any changes that happened on the cluster while the node was offline.
promises.plain: A crashed node can be restarted with no special steps, and it catches up on all writes the cluster committed while it was down.
promises.when_to_inject: SIGKILL a follower (and in other runs, the leader) in the middle of a steady stream of acknowledged writes. Keep writing to the surviving quorum, then restart the killed node with its original flags and data dir.
promises.outside_observation: After restart, run a level=none read on the restarted node itself (e.g. SELECT count(*), max(id)). Poll until it converges. Every write the cluster acknowledged, including those made while the node was down, must appear. No row may be missing or duplicated, and the restarted node must match the leader's strong read.
promises.workload_sketch: Start a 3-node cluster. Loop POST /db/execute INSERT INTO t(id,v) VALUES(?,?) with unique ids, logging acks to the Fuss history file. kill -9 node2. Continue inserts for N seconds. Restart node2 with the same -node-id, -raft-addr and data dir. Poll GET /db/query?level=none on node2 and compare with GET /db/query?level=strong on the leader.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a kill during snapshotting or WAL checkpointing could leave a partially written snapshot or SQLite file. Restart might then fail, or replay could skip or duplicate log entries.

promises.quote: You've now got a fault-tolerant, distributed, relational database. It can tolerate the failure of any node, even the Leader, and remain operational.
promises.plain: A 3-node cluster keeps accepting writes and reads after any one node, including the leader, is killed.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the current leader (found via GET /status or /nodes) while writes are in flight.
promises.outside_observation: After a bounded election window, writes sent to the surviving nodes succeed again. Every write acknowledged before the kill is still readable with level=strong. Writes that errored or timed out are recorded as indeterminate and are not counted as losses.
promises.workload_sketch: Start a 3-node cluster. Run concurrent clients doing INSERT with unique ids against all nodes. Find the leader via GET /nodes and kill -9 it. Keep writing to the remaining 2 nodes. After the run, do a strong SELECT and check that all acked ids are present.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: writes acknowledged by the old leader just before the kill might not have been committed by a quorum. That would be lost-ack data loss.

promises.quote: For a cluster of `N` nodes in size to remain operational, at least `(N/2)+1` nodes must be up and running, and be in contact with each other.
promises.plain: A cluster stays writable as long as a majority of voting nodes are up: 2 of 3, 3 of 5.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill exactly floor(N/2) voters, one at a time, during a write workload. In a 5-node cluster, kill 2 nodes, including the leader.
promises.outside_observation: With a majority still alive, writes continue to succeed after re-election. Acked data stays readable with level=strong on the survivors.
promises.workload_sketch: Start a 5-node cluster. Continuous INSERTs. kill -9 two voters, one of them the leader. Confirm POST /db/execute succeeds on a survivor within a timeout. Restart the killed nodes and verify convergence.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: two quick kills might land during an in-progress election. The survivors might then stay leaderless longer than expected or fail to converge.

promises.quote: A majority, or _Quorum_, of nodes within the cluster must concur on a given change for this operation to be successful.
promises.plain: A write must never be reported successful unless a majority of voters agreed to it, so writes cannot succeed when quorum is lost.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill 2 of 3 voters (or 2 of 4) and keep sending writes to the lone survivor.
promises.outside_observation: Every write sent while quorum is absent must return an error or time out, never success. After the killed nodes return, none of the errored writes may have silently appeared as acked. Errored writes that later appear are allowed as indeterminate but must be flagged.
promises.workload_sketch: Start a 3-node cluster. kill -9 node2 and node3. Send POST /db/execute INSERT id=X to node1 and record the response. Restart node2 and node3. Do a strong SELECT for X. A 200 response with no error on the INSERT while quorum was down is a violation.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a stale leader that has not yet noticed it lost followers might still answer, especially a level=none read or a queued write. It is unclear whether it could ever return success for a write.

promises.quote: Below is a table summarizing the quorum and fault tolerance for different cluster sizes:
promises.plain: A 4-node cluster tolerates only 1 failure, like a 3-node cluster, and a 2-node cluster tolerates 0.
promises.when_to_inject: In a 4-node cluster, kill 1 node (expect writes to continue), then a second (expect writes to stop). In a 2-node cluster, kill 1 (expect writes to stop).
promises.outside_observation: Write success or failure matches the table at each step. No write is acknowledged once the failure count exceeds the tolerance.
promises.workload_sketch: For each N in {2,3,4,5}: form the cluster, then loop {kill one more voter; attempt INSERT with a timeout; record ok/err}. Compare the results against the quorum table.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: with even N, a leader might keep serving briefly after losing quorum until its lease or heartbeat times out.

promises.quote: When it comes to the Raft protocol, these nodes do not count towards `N`, since they do not [vote](https://raft.github.io/).
promises.plain: Read replicas do not affect quorum: killing them never stops writes, and adding them never lets writes survive the loss of a voter majority.
promises.when_to_inject: Run 3 voters plus 3 read replicas (-raft-non-voter=true). Kill all replicas, then separately kill 2 voters while the replicas stay alive.
promises.outside_observation: Killing the replicas causes no write errors. Killing 2 voters makes writes fail even though 4 processes are still up. /nodes shows voter=false for replicas.
promises.workload_sketch: Start the voters, then join the replicas with -raft-non-voter=true -join. Continuous INSERTs. kill -9 all replicas and check the writes. Restart the replicas, then kill -9 two voters and check that writes now fail.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a misconfigured or misregistered replica might be counted as a voter in the configuration.

promises.quote: If a node receives a join request, and that node is not actually the Leader of the cluster, the receiving node will automatically redirect the requesting node to the Leader node. As a result a node can actually join a cluster by contacting any node in the cluster. You can also specify multiple join addresses, and the node will try each address until joining is successful.
promises.plain: A node can join by contacting any member, and if some listed join addresses are dead, it tries the others until it succeeds.
promises.when_to_inject: Before starting the joining node, kill the node listed first in -join, or kill the leader so the join target is a follower.
promises.outside_observation: The new node eventually appears in GET /nodes on the leader. It can serve level=none reads containing the existing data.
promises.workload_sketch: Start a 3-node cluster with some rows. kill -9 node1. Start node4 with -join host1:4002,host2:4002,host3:4002. Poll GET /nodes on node2 for node4. Query node4 with level=none.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the retry logic might give up after the first dead address or loop forever, or a redirect might point at a just-killed leader.

promises.quote: However, if a node does attempt to join a cluster it is already a member of, and neither its node ID nor its Raft network address has changed, then the cluster Leader will ignore the join request as there is nothing to do -- the joining node is already a fully configured member of the cluster.
promises.plain: Repeating a join with the same ID and Raft address is a no-op, so joins are idempotent.
promises.when_to_inject: Repeatedly kill and restart a member node, always passing -join, including restarts timed while the leader is changing.
promises.outside_observation: GET /nodes never shows duplicate entries for the node, cluster size stays constant, and writes are unaffected. The data on the rejoining node is preserved.
promises.workload_sketch: Start a 3-node cluster. Loop 20 times: kill -9 node3, then restart it with the same -node-id 3, -raft-addr and -join host1:4002. After each loop, GET /nodes and assert exactly 3 entries. Run an INSERT/SELECT.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a join racing with a leader change might be treated as new and cause a remove-then-add, briefly dropping quorum.

promises.quote: It is possible to change a node's Raft address between restarts. Simply pass the new address on the command line. **You must also, however, explicitly tell the node to join the cluster again, by passing `-join` to the node**. In this case what the Leader actually does is remove the previous record of the node, before adding a new record of the node.
promises.plain: Restarting a node with a new Raft address plus -join replaces its old record with the new address, without duplicating the node or losing data.
promises.when_to_inject: Stop a follower, then restart it on a different -raft-addr port with -join while writes continue. In a harder variant, kill the leader right after the rejoin.
promises.outside_observation: GET /nodes shows the node ID once, with the new address. Cluster size is unchanged. The node catches up on all acked writes.
promises.workload_sketch: Start a 3-node cluster with continuous INSERTs. kill node3. Restart with -node-id 3 -raft-addr host3:5002 -join host1:4002 using the same data dir. Poll GET /nodes. Do a level=none SELECT on node3 and compare with the leader.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: if the leader crashes between the remove and the add, the node might end up removed from the configuration entirely.

promises.quote: You can also change the HTTP API address of a node between restarts, but an explicit re-join is not required if just the HTTP API address changes.
promises.plain: Restarting a node on a new HTTP address without -join keeps it in the cluster, and it serves requests at the new address.
promises.when_to_inject: Stop a follower and restart it with a different -http-addr and no -join.
promises.outside_observation: The node answers on the new HTTP address. GET /nodes on the leader reports the updated API address eventually. Redirects or forwarded queries via that node work.
promises.workload_sketch: Start a 3-node cluster. kill node2. Restart it with -http-addr host2:5001 and the same raft-addr and data dir. GET /status on host2:5001. GET /nodes on the leader. Send an INSERT to node2 and verify it is forwarded and committed.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the leader might cache the old HTTP address, so redirects or forwarding from other nodes go to a dead address.

promises.quote: The new node will automatically pick up all changes that have occurred on the cluster since the cluster first started. In other words, after joining successfully, the new node will have a full copy of the SQLite database, just like every other node in the cluster.
promises.plain: A newly joined node eventually holds exactly the same database as the others.
promises.when_to_inject: Join a new node while writes are running, and kill the leader during the join or initial snapshot transfer.
promises.outside_observation: After convergence, a level=none read on the new node returns all acked rows, with no extras beyond indeterminate writes, matching a strong read on the leader.
promises.workload_sketch: Start a 3-node cluster and insert 100k rows (enough to trigger snapshots). Start node4 with -join while INSERTs continue. kill -9 the leader mid-join. Wait. Compare SELECT count(*), checksum-style aggregates on node4 at level=none against level=strong.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: an interrupted snapshot install might leave the new node with a partial database that is later treated as complete.

promises.quote: rqlite supports changing a node's role without removing it from the cluster. You can _promote_ a _[read replica](/docs/clustering/read-replicas/)_ to become a _voting_ node, and you can _demote_ a _voting_ node so that it becomes a _read replica_.
promises.plain: Promote and demote change a node's voter status while it stays a member with its data intact.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the leader right after sending POST /promote or /demote, or kill the target node during the call.
promises.outside_observation: GET /nodes shows the node still present, with a voter flag that is either fully old or fully new, never missing. Quorum behavior matches the reported role: after a demote in a 3-voter cluster, killing 1 other voter stops writes.
promises.workload_sketch: Start 3 voters plus 1 replica. POST /promote {"id":"4"} and immediately kill -9 the leader. After re-election, GET /nodes. Then POST /demote {"id":"4"} and verify the quorum math by killing voters.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a role-change configuration entry not yet committed when the leader dies might be lost while the client got a success response.

promises.quote: **Note that the cluster must be functional -- there must still be an operational Leader -- for this removal to be successful**. If, after a node failure, a given cluster does not have a quorum of nodes still running, you must bring back the failed node. Any attempt to remove it will fail as there will be no Leader to respond to the node-removal request.
promises.plain: Removing a node succeeds only when there is a leader. Without quorum, a remove request must fail and must not change the membership.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill 2 of 3 voters, then send DELETE /remove for one of them to the survivor.
promises.outside_observation: DELETE /remove returns an error. After the failed nodes are restarted, GET /nodes still lists all 3 nodes. With quorum present, a remove succeeds and the node disappears from /nodes.
promises.workload_sketch: Start a 3-node cluster. kill -9 node2 and node3. curl -XDELETE node1/remove -d '{"id":"3"}' and record the result. Restart node2 and node3. GET /nodes. Then, with quorum, kill node3 and remove it, and assert it is gone.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a remove sent to a stale leader might be appended locally and later committed, or the call might hang instead of failing.

promises.quote: If the node is shut down **gracefully** (it receives `SIGTERM` for example) it will first contact the Leader and remove itself from the cluster, and then the rqlite process will terminate. As a result the Leader will not continue to contact the node after it shuts down. This removal operation also reduces the cluster quorum size.
promises.plain: With -raft-cluster-remove-shutdown=true, SIGTERM removes the node from the cluster before exit and shrinks the quorum.
promises.when_to_inject: Send SIGTERM (graceful) to a node started with the flag, during writes. Compare with SIGKILL, which should leave the record in place.
promises.outside_observation: After SIGTERM, GET /nodes no longer lists the node. In a 3-node cluster that becomes 2 nodes, one further SIGTERM'd removal still leaves a writable single node, showing the quorum shrank. After SIGKILL, the node is still listed.
promises.workload_sketch: Start 3 nodes with -raft-cluster-remove-shutdown=true. Run INSERTs. kill -TERM node3 and wait for exit. GET /nodes and assert 2 entries. kill -TERM node2. Assert writes still succeed on node1. Repeat with kill -9 and assert the entry remains.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: if the node is the leader when it receives SIGTERM, self-removal might race with leadership transfer and the process might exit before the removal commits.

promises.quote: To enable reaping of voting nodes set `-raft-reap-node-timeout` to a non-zero time interval. Likewise, to enable reaping of read replicas set `-raft-reap-read-only-node-timeout`.
promises.plain: Nodes unreachable longer than the configured timeout are automatically removed, with voters and read replicas on separate timeouts.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill a replica and a voter (in a 5-node cluster) with short timeouts, e.g. 30s for replicas and 2m for voters. Step the clock of the leader's host forward or backward during the wait.
promises.outside_observation: The replica disappears from GET /nodes after about 30s, and the voter after about 2m, not before. Clock jumps should not cause premature reaping or indefinite delay. Reachable nodes are never reaped.
promises.workload_sketch: Start 5 voters plus 1 replica, all voters with -raft-reap-node-timeout=2m -raft-reap-read-only-node-timeout=30s. kill -9 the replica and one voter. Poll GET /nodes every 5s, recording removal times. In variants, skew the leader host's clock by +1h mid-wait.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: if the timeout uses wall-clock instead of monotonic time, a forward clock jump could reap healthy or briefly unreachable nodes immediately.

promises.quote: Note that the timeout clock is reset if a cluster elects a new Leader.
promises.plain: A leader election restarts the reap countdown, so a node is never reaped based on time counted by a previous leader.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill a node, wait about 80% of the reap timeout, then kill the leader to force an election.
promises.outside_observation: The dead node is not removed until a full timeout has elapsed after the new leader was elected, as seen from GET /nodes polling timestamps in the Fuss history.
promises.workload_sketch: Start 5 voters with -raft-reap-node-timeout=60s. kill -9 node5 at t0. At t0+50s, kill -9 the leader. Note the election time tE via GET /status. Poll GET /nodes and assert node5 is still present until at least tE+60s.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the new leader might inherit or derive last-contact times from replicated state rather than resetting them, reaping early.

promises.quote: For reaping to work consistently you **must** set these flags on **every** voting node in the cluster -- in other words, every node that could potentially become the Leader. You can also set the flags on read replicas, but they will simply be silently ignored.
promises.plain: Reaping happens only when the current leader has the flags, and flags on read replicas have no effect.
promises.when_to_inject: Configure the reap flags only on read replicas, or only on some voters, then kill a node and force leadership onto a voter without the flags.
promises.outside_observation: With flags only on replicas, no node is ever reaped. A node is reaped only while a flag-carrying voter is leader.
promises.workload_sketch: Start 3 voters without the flags plus 1 replica with -raft-reap-node-timeout=20s. kill -9 one voter. Wait 2 minutes and assert it is still in GET /nodes. In a second run, put the flag on node1 only, and kill leaders until node1 leads. Observe that reaping then occurs.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a replica might wrongly act on its flag, for example by issuing remove requests.

promises.quote: This log stores the set of committed SQLite commands, in the order in which they were executed. This log is the authoritative record of every change that has happened to the system.
promises.plain: Every acknowledged write is recorded in the Raft log, so it survives a crash.
promises.when_to_inject: SIGKILL all nodes, or the leader alone, while a stream of POST /db/execute requests is in flight. Repeat at random offsets, including immediately after a 200 response.
promises.outside_observation: Fuss's own history file lists every write that received a 200 response with no error in the results. After restart and /readyz returning OK, read with GET /db/query?level=strong. Every acknowledged row must be present. Unacknowledged rows may be either present or absent.
promises.workload_sketch: Run POST /db/execute ["CREATE TABLE t(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, v TEXT)"]. Then loop POST /db/execute [["INSERT INTO t(id,v) VALUES(?,?)", n, uuid]], logging the response for each n. Kill -9 and restart rqlited with the same -node-id and data dir. Run GET /db/query?level=strong&q=SELECT id,v FROM t. Diff the result against the acknowledged set.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a response might be sent after commit but before the log entry is fsync'd on a majority, or a full-cluster kill might lose a tail that was acknowledged.

promises.quote: This log stores the set of committed SQLite commands, in the order in which they were executed.
promises.plain: Committed writes are applied in the same order they were committed, including across leader failover.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the leader between two sequential, acknowledged, order-dependent writes, then keep writing to the new leader.
promises.outside_observation: One client issues serial updates and waits for each acknowledgement. The final value and the append-only log table must match the client's acknowledgement order. Fuss checks that no later-acknowledged write is overwritten by an earlier one and that the sequence column is monotonic in id order.
promises.workload_sketch: Single client loop: POST /db/execute [["UPDATE c SET v=? WHERE k=1", i], ["INSERT INTO log(seq) VALUES(?)", i]] with i increasing. Kill the leader mid-run and follow redirects to the new leader. At the end, SELECT v FROM c must equal the last acknowledged i, and SELECT seq FROM log ORDER BY rowid must be increasing.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a request the client retries after a timeout during failover might be applied twice or out of order, because the HTTP API has no idempotency key.

promises.quote: Since every node in an rqlite cluster applies the log entries in exactly the same way, this guarantees that the SQLite database is the same on every node.
promises.plain: After faults settle, every node's SQLite contents are identical.
promises.when_to_inject: Randomly kill and restart followers and leaders during a mixed write workload. Then stop the faults and wait for all nodes to report the same applied index in /status.
promises.outside_observation: Query each node directly with GET /db/query?level=none. Run SELECT * ORDER BY id and a checksum aggregate. Results must be byte-identical across nodes. Fuss can also copy each node's SQLite file read-only and compare query results offline.
promises.workload_sketch: Start 3 nodes. Run concurrent INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE through POST /db/execute while a fault loop kill -9's a random node every few seconds and restarts it. Quiesce, poll /status until the raft applied_index values are equal, then compare SELECT count(*), sum(id), group_concat(v) on each node with level=none.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: non-deterministic SQL such as random() or datetime('now') under clock skew could make nodes diverge if it is evaluated per node rather than rewritten before logging.

promises.quote: However, this configuration risks database corruption in the event of a crash. To address this risk, rqlite periodically switches SQLite to `SYNCHRONOUS=FULL` mode, thereby fsync'ing the entire SQLite database to disk.
promises.plain: A crash at any point, including during the periodic fsync, does not leave the node with a corrupt database.
promises.when_to_inject: SIGKILL repeatedly at random moments under heavy write load, so that some kills land during the periodic SYNCHRONOUS=FULL fsync or a snapshot.
promises.outside_observation: After restart the node becomes ready via /readyz. PRAGMA integrity_check, run through /db/query, returns 'ok'. The data matches the acknowledged history. A node that refuses to start or returns SQLite errors is a failure.
promises.workload_sketch: High-rate POST /db/execute inserts with large blobs. Kill -9 at random intervals, restart, and wait for /readyz. Run GET /db/query?level=strong&q=PRAGMA integrity_check and diff the rows against acknowledged writes. Repeat hundreds of times.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a kill landing exactly while the mode is switched to FULL or back to OFF might leave a WAL/DB pair that looks valid but is torn.

promises.quote: When rqlite restarts, it starts from the last known fsync'ed version of the SQLite database. In the event that no such copy is available (or if there is any question about its correctness) the SQLite database is completely rebuilt using the information stored in the Raft log.
promises.plain: After restart, the database contains every committed change, whether it was recovered from the last fsync'd copy or rebuilt from the Raft log.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill -9 at three points: just after a burst of writes and before the next periodic fsync, during an fsync, and while the data directory is near-full. Restart each time.
promises.outside_observation: After restart, every acknowledged write is visible and no unacknowledged-then-rejected write appears. Fuss can observe the restart path by reading file timestamps in the data dir and comparing startup duration. Correctness is checked purely via query results.
promises.workload_sketch: Write N rows, then kill -9 immediately after the last 200 response. Restart and run SELECT count(*), max(id) with level=strong. Compare against Fuss's history. Variant: kill during the restart itself, while the rebuild is in progress, then restart again and re-check.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the 'any question about its correctness' check might miss a stale but structurally valid SQLite file. The node would then start from it and skip the Raft entries after it.

promises.quote: When rqlite restarts, it starts from the last known fsync'ed version of the SQLite database. In the event that no such copy is available (or if there is any question about its correctness) the SQLite database is completely rebuilt using the information stored in the Raft log.
promises.plain: Running out of disk during writes or fsync must not lead to acknowledged data loss or a corrupt database after space is restored and the node restarts.
promises.when_to_inject: Fill the filesystem holding -data-dir, using a small loopback or tmpfs mount, while writes and periodic fsync/snapshot are occurring.
promises.outside_observation: Writes either fail with an error or succeed. Anything that got a 200 response must be present after freeing space and restarting. PRAGMA integrity_check returns ok, and /readyz recovers.
promises.workload_sketch: Mount a small filesystem as the data dir and start rqlited. Insert large rows until the API returns errors, logging every response. Free space, then kill -9 and restart. Query with level=strong and run integrity_check. Diff against acknowledged rows.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: ENOSPC during the SQLite fsync or snapshot write might be logged but not surfaced, leaving a partial snapshot that is trusted on restart.

promises.quote: rqlite automatically performs log compaction, so that disk usage due to the log remains bounded. After a configurable number of changes, rqlite snapshots the SQLite database and truncates the Raft log.
promises.plain: Raft log disk usage stays bounded through snapshots and truncation, and crashing during this does not lose data.
promises.when_to_inject: Set a low -raft-snap threshold so snapshots happen frequently. Kill -9 at random times so some kills land mid-snapshot or mid-truncation.
promises.outside_observation: Fuss reads file sizes in the data dir (raft log file and snapshot directory) and checks they plateau rather than grow linearly with the number of writes. After each kill and restart, every acknowledged row is present and integrity_check is ok.
promises.workload_sketch: Start rqlited with -raft-snap=100. Run a long loop of small UPDATEs on a fixed-size table, sampling data dir file sizes every second. Inject kill -9 periodically and restart. Assert sizes are bounded and the data is correct.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a crash after log truncation but before the snapshot is fully persisted could leave neither source with the truncated entries.

promises.quote: Only one node can bootstrap a cluster, so any other node that attempts to do so later will fail, and instead become a _Follower_ in the new cluster.
promises.plain: With automatic bootstrapping, exactly one cluster forms with exactly one bootstrapping node, and all others join as followers.
promises.when_to_inject: Start all N nodes with -bootstrap-expect at the same instant. In variants, kill and restart one node during the bootstrap window, or delay starts by random amounts.
promises.outside_observation: GET /nodes and /status on every node show the same single leader and the same membership set. There are never two disjoint clusters and never two leaders in the same term. A write to one node is readable at level=strong from every node.
promises.workload_sketch: Start 3 rqlited processes concurrently, each with -bootstrap-expect 3 -join a,b,c. Poll /nodes on each until stable, then check that the membership and leader agree. POST a write and read it back from all nodes. Repeat many times with random start jitter and kills.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: two nodes might each reach the -bootstrap-expect contact count at nearly the same moment and both bootstrap, producing a split cluster.

promises.quote: Each node attempts to atomically set a special key (the node writes its HTTP and Raft network addresses as the value for the key). Only one node will succeed in doing this and will then declare itself Leader, and other nodes will then join with it.
promises.plain: With Consul or etcd discovery, only one node wins the leader key and all others join it.
promises.when_to_inject: Start all nodes simultaneously against a fresh Consul/etcd instance that Fuss runs itself. Variant: kill the winning node right after it sets the key, then restart it.
promises.outside_observation: Fuss reads the key in Consul/etcd and /nodes on each rqlite node. Exactly one cluster forms, and its leader matches the address stored in the key at formation time.
promises.workload_sketch: Run etcd locally. Start 3 rqlited with -disco-mode etcd-kv and the matching -disco-config at the same time. Read the etcd key and poll /nodes on each node. Assert a single cluster and a write visible on all nodes.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: if the key-setter crashes before its Raft layer bootstraps, other nodes may keep trying to join a dead address, or a stale key may be reused after restart.

promises.quote: To prevent multiple nodes updating the Leader key at once, nodes use a check-and-set operation, only updating the special key if its value has not changed since it was last read by the node.
promises.plain: Concurrent updates to the Consul/etcd leader key never overwrite one another, because each update is check-and-set.
promises.when_to_inject: Force leader changes, by killing the leader repeatedly, while several nodes are alive and racing to update the key.
promises.outside_observation: Fuss watches the key's revision history in etcd/Consul. Each update must be based on the previous revision, and the final key value must match the leader reported by /status on the nodes.
promises.workload_sketch: Run a 3-node cluster with -disco-mode etcd-kv. Loop: kill the current leader (found via /status), wait for a new leader, then compare the etcd key history (watch with revisions) with /status. Restart the killed node and repeat.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a node waking from a pause, for example under clock skew or SIGSTOP, might write a stale leader address if it re-reads the key before the CAS.

promises.quote: By using Raft, rqlite prevents divergent copies of the data, and ensures there is one authoritative, consistent copy of that data at all times.
promises.plain: No two nodes ever end up with conflicting committed data, even across crashes and leader changes.
promises.when_to_inject: Repeatedly SIGKILL the current Leader (found via GET /status or /nodes) while a stream of writes is in flight. Then restart it. Optionally combine with clock skew on one node.
promises.outside_observation: After the cluster quiesces, query every node with level=none. Each node must return exactly the same table contents in the same order of applied writes. Every acknowledged write must appear on every node. No node may hold a row that another node's committed history contradicts.
promises.workload_sketch: Start 3 rqlited nodes (-node-id, -http-addr, -raft-addr, -bootstrap-expect 3 / -join). POST /db/execute CREATE TABLE t(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, v TEXT). Loop: POST /db/execute INSERT INTO t(id,v) VALUES(n,'x'), recording each ack or error in Fuss's history file. Kill the leader every few seconds, then restart it with the same -node-id and data dir. Finally GET /db/query?q=SELECT * FROM t ORDER BY id&level=none on each node and diff the results.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a node killed after appending log entries it never got committed could apply them locally during its restart replay before it learns the new leader's log, briefly exposing divergent data to level=none reads.

promises.quote: Yes, this is an intrinsic part of the Raft protocol.
promises.plain: A write is acknowledged only after a quorum has accepted it, so an acknowledged write survives the Leader crashing.
promises.when_to_inject: Immediately after the Leader returns HTTP 200 for a write. Kill the Leader (and optionally one follower in a 5-node cluster) before it can do anything else.
promises.outside_observation: Once a new Leader is elected, every acknowledged write must be readable with level=strong. A write that Fuss recorded as acknowledged but that is now missing means the promise was broken.
promises.workload_sketch: 3-node cluster. Loop: POST /db/execute INSERT unique id. On HTTP 200 with no 'error' field in results, record it as acked, then immediately SIGKILL the leader. Wait for a leader in /status on the survivors. GET /db/query?level=strong&q=SELECT id FROM t and check that every acked id is present. Restart the killed node and repeat.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the HTTP response might be sent after local apply but with a window where fsync of the Raft log on followers is not complete, so a correlated kill loses the entry.

promises.quote: Yes, this is an intrinsic part of the Raft protocol.
promises.plain: If the Leader's disk is full, writes must fail with an error rather than be acknowledged and later lost.
promises.when_to_inject: Fill the filesystem holding the Leader's -data-dir (for example, a small tmpfs or loop mount) while writes are ongoing.
promises.outside_observation: Each write either returns an error or is acknowledged. Every acknowledged write must still be present after space is freed and the nodes are restarted.
promises.workload_sketch: Run the Leader on a 50MB loop-mounted data dir. Insert rows containing large blobs until writes start erroring, recording the status of each. Free space, restart all nodes, then SELECT and confirm all acked rows exist and the database is readable.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a failed Raft log or snapshot write might be logged but not surfaced to the client, or a partial snapshot file might prevent restart.

promises.quote: If a client sends a write-request to a node and that node is not the Leader, the node will transparently forward the request to the Leader, wait for a response, and then return the response to the client. If the node receiving the write cannot contact the Leader (which shouldn't happen during normal operation, as all functional clusters have a Leader), the write will fail and return an error to the client.
promises.plain: A write sent to a follower is applied through the Leader, and if no Leader is reachable the client gets an error instead of a false success.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the Leader (or a majority of nodes) while writes are being sent to a follower.
promises.outside_observation: Each follower response is either a success whose row later appears cluster-wide, or an error. A success whose row never appears is a violation. A write that returned an error but appears anyway is allowed (indeterminate), but Fuss should log it as worth checking.
promises.workload_sketch: 3-node cluster. Send all INSERTs only to follower F via POST /db/execute. Kill the leader mid-stream, and in a second run kill both other nodes. Record the responses. After restart, SELECT on all nodes and reconcile against Fuss's history.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the follower could time out waiting for the forwarded response and report an error after the Leader actually committed the write, or report success based on a stale leader connection.

promises.quote: If a read request must be serviced by the Leader, however, rqlite will transparently forward the request to the Leader, wait for the Leader to handle it, and return the results to the client. If the node receiving the read cannot contact the Leader (which shouldn't happen during normal operation, as all functional clusters have a Leader), the read will fail and return an error to the client.
promises.plain: Leader-required reads sent to a follower either return the Leader's up-to-date answer or fail with an error; they never silently return stale data.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the Leader or a majority of nodes while level=strong (or level=weak) reads are sent to a follower.
promises.outside_observation: Each strong read returns data reflecting every write acknowledged before the read started, or returns an error. A stale success is a violation.
promises.workload_sketch: Write an incrementing counter row via the leader, recording the acked values. Concurrently GET /db/query?level=strong&q=SELECT v FROM c on a follower. Kill the leader, then kill the majority. Check that no successful read returned a value lower than the latest value acked before that read began.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a deposed Leader that has not yet noticed it lost leadership might serve a forwarded read from its own stale state.

promises.quote: Some reads, depending on the requested [_read consistency_](/docs/api/read-consistency/), do not need to be serviced by the Leader, and in that case the node can service the read regardless of whether it can contact the Leader or not.
promises.plain: Reads with level=none still succeed on a node even when no Leader is reachable.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill all nodes except one in a 3-node cluster.
promises.outside_observation: GET /db/query?level=none on the surviving node returns HTTP 200 with data instead of an error. The data must be a prefix of the acknowledged history, never containing unacknowledged rows that were later lost.
promises.workload_sketch: Insert rows. Kill 2 of 3 nodes. Repeatedly GET /db/query?level=none&q=SELECT * FROM t on the survivor and record the result. Restart the other nodes and compare.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the survivor might reject all queries while it is in candidate state.

promises.quote: This means that if an rqlite cluster is partitioned, only the side of the cluster that contains a majority of the nodes will be available. The other side of the cluster will not respond to writes. However the side that remains available will return consistent results, and when the partition is healed, consistent results will continue to be returned.
promises.plain: A minority of nodes must refuse writes, and once the majority returns the results stay consistent.
promises.when_to_inject: Approximate a partition by killing a majority (2 of 3 nodes), leaving one node up. Then restart the killed nodes to simulate healing.
promises.outside_observation: Writes to the lone node return an error or time out, and none of them appear later as committed. After restart, all nodes agree and every pre-fault acknowledged write is present.
promises.workload_sketch: 3 nodes. Insert rows A. Kill 2 nodes. POST /db/execute INSERT rows B to the survivor and expect errors. Restart the 2 nodes. Query all nodes with level=strong and level=none: A must be present, and any B that errored must not be present unless Fuss classified it as indeterminate.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a write accepted into the lone node's local log before it noticed loss of quorum might be committed after the heal, despite having returned an error or timeout.

promises.quote: However if the client is on the other side of the partition, one of two things will happen. The client may be redirected to the Leader, but will then (presumably) fail to contact the Leader due to the partition, and experience a timeout. Alternatively the client may receive a `no leader` error.
promises.plain: A client talking to a node without quorum sees either a timeout or a 'no leader' error, not a success.
promises.when_to_inject: After killing a majority of the cluster.
promises.outside_observation: The HTTP response from the surviving node is a timeout or an error body containing 'no leader' or similar, never a 200 with successful results.
promises.workload_sketch: Kill 2 of 3 nodes. POST /db/execute to the survivor with a client timeout. Classify each response as timeout, error, or success.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the error text may differ ('leadership lost', 'not leader'), which would not be a safety violation, so Fuss should only flag successes.

promises.quote: Of course, you won't have any redundancy or fault tolerance if you only run a single node. If the single node fails you will need to restart it.
promises.plain: A single-node cluster that is killed and restarted keeps all writes it acknowledged.
promises.when_to_inject: SIGKILL the single rqlited process at random moments during writes, including during snapshots (lower the snapshot threshold via the documented snapshot flags so snapshots happen often).
promises.outside_observation: After restarting with the same data dir, every acknowledged row is present and the node accepts writes again.
promises.workload_sketch: Start a single node with a small -raft-snap threshold. Loop INSERTs and record the acks. SIGKILL at a random time. Restart with the same flags. SELECT all rows and compare against the acks. Repeat many times.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: being killed mid-snapshot or mid-WAL-checkpoint could leave a partial snapshot that fails to load, or lose entries truncated from the log.

promises.quote: A 3-node cluster, in which two nodes fail, is not a single-node cluster. In that case you've still got a 3-node cluster, but one which is offline due to lack of quorum.
promises.plain: With 2 of 3 nodes dead, the remaining node must not act as a Leader or accept writes, even after it restarts.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill 2 nodes, then also restart the third node on its own.
promises.outside_observation: GET /status on the survivor never reports it as Leader, and writes to it are rejected.
promises.workload_sketch: 3 nodes. Kill 2. Restart the third with its original flags. Poll /status for its raft state. POST /db/execute and expect failure.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a restarted node whose peer configuration was lost or mis-read could bootstrap itself as a 1-node cluster.

promises.quote: Yes. If a client sends a write request to a [read replica](/docs/clustering/read-replicas/), the replica transparently forwards the request to the Leader -- the client doesn't need to know it isn't talking to the Leader. This also makes read replicas an effective messaging fabric: a client at the edge can write a change via its local replica, and that change will be replicated to every other node connected to the cluster.
promises.plain: A write sent to a read replica is committed through the Leader and eventually appears on every node, including other replicas.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the Leader or the replica while writes are being sent via the replica. Restart afterward.
promises.outside_observation: Every write the replica acknowledged eventually appears on all voters and all replicas when queried with level=none. Writes that returned an error may appear only if Fuss marked them indeterminate.
promises.workload_sketch: 3 voters plus 2 read-only nodes (-raft-non-voter=true). INSERT via replica R1. Kill the leader mid-stream, then also kill and restart R1. Query all 5 nodes with level=none after quiescence and compare against Fuss's history.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a replica restarted from its data dir might not catch up on entries committed while it was down, if snapshot install fails.

promises.quote: You can wrap a bulk update in a transaction such that all the statements in the bulk request will succeed, or none of them will.
promises.plain: A bulk request sent with transaction=true is applied entirely or not at all, even if a node crashes during it.
promises.when_to_inject: SIGKILL the Leader while a large transactional bulk request is in flight, or right after it is acknowledged.
promises.outside_observation: After restart, each bulk batch (tagged with a batch id in every row) is either fully present or fully absent. A partial batch is a violation. Also, a batch containing a deliberately failing statement must leave no rows.
promises.workload_sketch: POST /db/execute?transaction with a JSON array of 1000 INSERTs sharing batch_id=k. Include some batches whose last statement violates a constraint. Kill the leader at random. Restart, then SELECT batch_id, count(*) FROM t GROUP BY batch_id. Each count must be 0 or 1000, and failing batches must be 0.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a crash during SQLite apply after a Raft commit, replayed on restart, might interact badly with a snapshot taken mid-apply and leave a partial batch.

promises.quote:
Is the underlying serializable isolation level of SQLite maintained?
Yes, it is.
promises.plain: Concurrent operations behave as if executed in some serial order.
promises.when_to_inject: Throughout a run with many concurrent clients, combined with leader kills.
promises.outside_observation: Fuss's recorded history of transfers and strong reads passes a serializability checker. For example, the total balance across accounts is always constant in strong reads, and no read observes a partially applied transactional bulk request.
promises.workload_sketch: Accounts table. Clients send transactional bulk requests: UPDATE a SET bal=bal-1 WHERE id=x; UPDATE a SET bal=bal+1 WHERE id=y. Readers send GET /db/query?level=strong&q=SELECT sum(bal) FROM a. Kill the leader periodically. Check that the sum is invariant and feed the history to an Elle-style checker.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: reads served by a newly elected Leader before it applies all committed entries might observe a prefix that does not line up with acknowledged writes.

promises.quote: There is also a more fundamental reason too -- the Raft log serializes all writes, so even if SQLite supported concurrent updates, the Raft system would prevent writers taking advantage of it.
promises.plain: All writes are applied in one total order that is the same on every node.
promises.when_to_inject: Send many concurrent writes to different nodes while killing and restarting nodes.
promises.outside_observation: Each write appends a row using an AUTOINCREMENT id plus the client tag. After quiescence, the (id, tag) sequence is identical on every node, and each client's own writes appear in the order that client received acks.
promises.workload_sketch: Many clients each POST /db/execute INSERT INTO log(tag) VALUES('cX-n') to random nodes. Kill and restart nodes randomly. Finally SELECT id, tag FROM log ORDER BY id on all nodes and compare the sequences, and check per-client ack order.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: forwarded writes retried internally after a leader change could be applied twice or out of order relative to the client's acks.

promises.quote: No, a read does not block other reads, nor does a read block a write -- as long as the reads do not use the _Strong_ consistency level.
promises.plain: Long-running non-strong reads should not stall writes (apart from brief snapshot pauses).
promises.when_to_inject: While many long-running level=weak or level=none queries are executing.
promises.outside_observation: Write latency stays bounded (no write waits for the full duration of a long read), except for short stalls that line up with snapshots.
promises.workload_sketch: Run many concurrent GET /db/query?level=none with an expensive SELECT (for example, a cross join). Concurrently time POST /db/execute INSERTs. Compare write latency distributions with and without the reads, using a low snapshot threshold.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a long read holding a SQLite read transaction could block snapshotting, which then blocks writes for the full duration of the read, not just milliseconds.

promises.quote: This means that any application talking to rqlite shouldn't notice if a node fails because other nodes in the cluster automatically take over.
promises.plain: Losing one node in a 3-node cluster leaves the cluster available for reads and writes after a brief failover.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill any single node, including the Leader, during steady load.
promises.outside_observation: Writes and strong reads sent to the surviving nodes resume succeeding within a bounded failover window, and no acknowledged data is lost.
promises.workload_sketch: 3 nodes, continuous INSERTs and strong SELECTs spread across nodes. Kill one node. Measure the gap until success resumes, and verify all acks are present afterward.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: clients pinned to the killed node will obviously fail, and leader election plus forwarding reconnection may take seconds, so 'shouldn't notice' is only true with retries elsewhere.

promises.quote: rqlite supports hot backups, so you can back up a node while it is running.
promises.plain: A backup taken while writes are in flight is a valid SQLite file holding a consistent snapshot of the database.
promises.when_to_inject: Run a steady stream of acknowledged INSERTs through /db/execute while GET /db/backup is streaming.
promises.outside_observation: The downloaded file passes PRAGMA integrity_check. Its rows are a prefix-closed set of Fuss's acknowledged writes: every write acked before the backup request started is present, and no unacknowledged or torn write appears.
promises.workload_sketch: CREATE TABLE t(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, v); loop: POST /db/execute INSERT id=n, log ack to history; concurrently: GET /db/backup -o b.sqlite3 repeatedly; open each with sqlite3, run integrity_check, and compare ids to history.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a WAL-mode copy could be taken between a WAL write and a checkpoint, giving a file that is missing frames or fails the integrity check.
