promises.quote: In either case the generated file can then be used to restore a node (or cluster) using the restore API.
promises.plain: A backup taken under load can be booted or loaded into a fresh node, and that node then serves exactly the backup's contents.
promises.when_to_inject: Take the backup while writes are in flight, then restore it into a fresh node.
promises.outside_observation: SELECT on the restored node returns the same rows as reading the backup file directly with sqlite3.
promises.workload_sketch: Write load on node A; GET /db/backup -o b.sqlite3 from A; start a fresh single node B; POST /boot with b.sqlite3; SELECT * FROM t on B; diff against sqlite3 b.sqlite3.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the default WAL-mode file might carry WAL state that is lost or mishandled on boot.

promises.quote: Instead **if** the stream is interrupted the node will set the Trailing HTTP header `X-STREAM-ERROR`.
promises.plain: If a backup stream fails partway, the response carries an X-Stream-Error trailer instead of looking like a clean, complete download.
promises.when_to_inject: Fill the data-directory filesystem just before or during a GET /db/backup?fmt=delete or ?vacuum request, since both need an extra on-disk copy.
promises.outside_observation: Every response is one of three things: a complete file that passes integrity_check, a response with the X-Stream-Error trailer set, or a transport-level error. A truncated or invalid body with a clean chunked terminator and no trailer is a violation.
promises.workload_sketch: Load roughly 50MB of data; fill the disk to near-full with a filler file; curl --raw GET /db/backup?fmt=delete and capture the body and trailers; validate the body with sqlite3.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: an error during the temporary-copy phase might happen before streaming starts and produce an empty body with HTTP 200 and no trailer.

promises.quote: Requesting a DELETE mode backup involves making a copy of the SQLite database so ensure you have sufficient disk space or the backup may fail.
promises.plain: Without enough disk space a DELETE-mode backup fails visibly, and the node keeps working afterward.
promises.when_to_inject: While the extra copy for fmt=delete is being made.
promises.outside_observation: The failure is visible (trailer or error), no corrupt file is presented as success, and once space is freed the node still accepts writes and reads with its data intact.
promises.workload_sketch: Fill the disk; GET /db/backup?fmt=delete; free the space; POST /db/execute INSERT; GET /db/query SELECT count(*); compare with history.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a leftover temp copy might stay on disk, or a failed copy might wedge the store.

promises.quote: Note that if the node is not the Leader, the node will transparently forward the request to the Leader, wait for the backup data from the Leader, and return it to the client.
promises.plain: A backup requested from a follower returns the leader's full, valid database, or fails visibly.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the leader while the follower is forwarding a backup request.
promises.outside_observation: The follower's response is either a complete, valid backup containing all writes acked before the request, or a visible error or trailer. It is never a silently partial file. Repeating the request after the new election succeeds.
promises.workload_sketch: Start a 3-node cluster; write rows; GET follower:/db/backup; at the same moment, SIGKILL the leader; validate the result; retry the GET after the new leader appears.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the proxy may relay a truncated leader stream with a clean termination.

promises.quote: In that case if a Follower receives a backup request the Follower will respond with HTTP 301 Moved Permanently and include the address of the Leader as the `Location` header in the response.
promises.plain: With ?redirect, a follower answers 301, and the Location header points at the current leader.
promises.when_to_inject: Right after killing and restarting the leader, which forces a leadership change.
promises.outside_observation: The Location header matches the leader reported by /status after the election. It must not point at the dead node.
promises.workload_sketch: Start a 3-node cluster; kill the leader; wait for the election; GET follower:/db/backup?redirect; compare Location with the leader shown in /status.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the follower may cache a stale leader address for a while after the election.

promises.quote: rqlite writes a **compressed** copy of its SQLite database, and will not create a backup if the SQLite database hasn't changed since the last upload took place.
promises.plain: Auto-backup skips uploading when nothing has changed since the last upload, including across a node restart.
promises.when_to_inject: Restart the node after an upload, with no writes in between.
promises.outside_observation: With type=file and timestamp:true, count the files in the backup dir. No new timestamped file should appear in intervals with no writes, before or after the restart. Note that the restart case is an inference: the spec does not say whether the 'last upload' memory survives a restart.
promises.workload_sketch: Point -auto-backup at a file config with interval 5s, timestamp true, and a Fuss-readable dir; write once; wait for one file; idle for 30s and count files; restart rqlited; idle for 30s and count again.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the 'last upload' marker may be kept only in memory, so a restart forces a redundant upload.

promises.quote: Only the Leader performs the backup. If a new node becomes the Leader it will take over the backup process.
promises.plain: Only one node, the leader, uploads auto-backups, and after a leader dies the new leader keeps producing backups that include later writes.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the leader between backup intervals while writes continue.
promises.outside_observation: Give each node its own backup dir. Only the current leader's dir gains new files. After the kill, the new leader's dir gains files whose decompressed contents include writes acked after the kill.
promises.workload_sketch: Start 3 nodes, each with a file auto-backup config (interval 5s, timestamp true, separate dir); write continuously; SIGKILL the leader; keep writing; gunzip the newest file from the new leader and check it for the post-kill ids.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the backup goroutine may start only at boot, so a node promoted later never begins uploading.

promises.quote: To enable timestamping add `timestamp: true` ... which will result in a new backup file being created each time. ... `TIMESTAMP` will be in the form `YYYYMMDDHHMMSS`, UTC timezone.
promises.plain: With timestamping, every upload creates a new, distinct UTC-timestamped file and never overwrites an earlier one.
promises.when_to_inject: Step the leader's clock backward between uploads, or forward and then back.
promises.outside_observation: The number of files equals the number of uploads, and no earlier file's contents change. Name collisions or overwrites after the backward clock step are violations. Names must match the UTC YYYYMMDDHHMMSS form.
promises.workload_sketch: Use a file config with interval 2s and timestamp true; write between intervals; record a hash of each file; step the clock back 1 hour; keep writing; check that the file count only grows and that old hashes are unchanged.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: names come straight from wall-clock time, so a backward step can regenerate an existing name and overwrite that backup.

promises.quote: In the example above, rqlite will check every 5 minutes if an upload is required, and do so if needed.
promises.plain: Auto-backup checks on the configured interval and uploads whenever data has changed, even if the wall clock jumps.
promises.when_to_inject: Jump the clock forward or backward by a large amount while auto-backup is running.
promises.outside_observation: After the jump, a write is still followed by a new backup within about one interval of real elapsed time.
promises.workload_sketch: Use a file config with interval 5s; jump the clock back 1 day; INSERT a row; wait 15s of real time; check that a new or updated backup contains the row.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: if the scheduler compares wall-clock timestamps instead of using a monotonic timer, a backward jump could stall uploads.

promises.quote: However, if you do decide to _Load_ or _Boot_ a system with a SQLite binary file, any existing data will be replaced in its entirety by the operation.
promises.plain: After a successful load or boot of a SQLite file, the node holds exactly that file's data, with nothing left over from before, and this survives a restart.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill and restart the node immediately after the load or boot returns success.
promises.outside_observation: After the restart, the node's rows equal the loaded file's rows exactly. No pre-existing rows or tables remain.
promises.workload_sketch: Create table old and insert rows; POST /db/load with Content-type application/octet-stream and restore.sqlite; on 200, SIGKILL and restart; SELECT from sqlite_master and foo; diff against restore.sqlite.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the load might be acked before it is durably snapshotted or logged, so a crash rolls the node back to the old data.

promises.quote: any existing data will be replaced in its entirety by the operation.
promises.plain: A load or boot interrupted by a crash should never leave a mix of old and new data. Note that the spec states the replace-in-entirety outcome only for a completed operation, so this crash-mid-operation check is Fuss's inference.
promises.when_to_inject: Partway through streaming a large file to /boot or /db/load.
promises.outside_observation: After the restart, the node has either only the old data or only the new data. Mixed tables, or a node that fails to start with a corrupt store, are suspicious.
promises.workload_sketch: Seed old data; POST /boot with a 500MB file; SIGKILL midway; restart; inspect sqlite_master and row counts.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: boot may write the database file in place before swapping it in, so a crash leaves a torn file.

promises.quote: You can send _Load_ requests to any node in your cluster and that node will transparently forward the request to the Leader if necessary.
promises.plain: A load sent to a follower is applied once, cluster-wide, or fails visibly.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the leader while a follower is forwarding a load request.
promises.outside_observation: If the load returned success, every surviving node eventually serves the loaded data. If it failed, a retry yields the loaded data with no mixed state.
promises.workload_sketch: Start a 3-node cluster; POST follower:/db/load with a SQLite file; SIGKILL the leader at the same moment; after the election, read from all nodes with level=strong and compare.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the forwarded request may be applied on the old leader but its success never relayed, so the client sees an error for a load that actually happened.

promises.quote: If enabled and **the node has no pre-existing data**, rqlite will download the SQLite data stored in the cloud, and initialize your system with it.
promises.plain: Auto-restore runs only on an empty node, so restarting a node that already has data must not overwrite it with the cloud backup.
promises.when_to_inject: Restart a node with -auto-restore after it has accepted writes made since the initial restore.
promises.outside_observation: Writes acknowledged before the restart are still present afterward. The node is not reset to the backup's contents.
promises.workload_sketch: Run local MinIO holding backup B; start rqlited with -auto-restore pointing at MinIO; confirm B's data; INSERT new rows; SIGKILL; restart with the same flags; SELECT and confirm the new rows are present.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the 'pre-existing data' check might look only at the SQLite file and not the Raft log or snapshots, so it misjudges a crashed node as empty.

promises.quote: Also note that if you bootstrap a new cluster and pass `-auto-restore` to each node, only the node that becomes the Leader will actually install the data. The other nodes will pick up the data through the normal Raft consensus mechanism.
promises.plain: In a fresh cluster with auto-restore on every node, the data is installed once and all nodes converge to the same contents, with no duplicates.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the first leader shortly after cluster bootstrap, during or right after its restore.
promises.outside_observation: All surviving nodes eventually return identical row sets equal to the backup. There are no duplicated or missing rows, and no node is stuck empty.
promises.workload_sketch: Run MinIO holding backup B; start 3 nodes with -auto-restore and -bootstrap-expect 3; SIGKILL the leader right after election; restart it; read from each node with level=none and diff against B.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a second node that becomes leader after the crash may also see 'no data' and install the backup again, racing with the replicated copy.

promises.quote: By default rqlite will exit with an error if it fails to download the backup file. If you wish an rqlite node to continue starting up even if the download fails, set `continue_on_failure: true`.
promises.plain: If the backup download fails, rqlite exits with an error by default, and keeps starting up only when continue_on_failure is true.
promises.when_to_inject: Make the S3 endpoint unreachable (stop the local MinIO) before starting rqlited with -auto-restore.
promises.outside_observation: With false, the process exits with a non-zero code and the HTTP API never comes up. With true, the process stays up and /status responds with an empty database.
promises.workload_sketch: Stop MinIO; start rqlited -auto-restore with continue_on_failure false and record the exit code; repeat with true and poll GET /status.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a hung download might hit neither an error nor the timeout path, so the node blocks forever instead of exiting or continuing.

promises.quote: When a node starts, rqlite computes a [CRC checksum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclic_redundancy_check) over every on-disk data file and compares it to a value that was stored when rqlite originally wrote the file (this value is stored in a _sidecar_ file). The node refuses to run if any file fails the check.
promises.plain: On startup a node verifies every data file against its sidecar CRC and refuses to run if any file does not match.
promises.when_to_inject: SIGKILL the node while it is writing data files: during a burst of writes, during a snapshot triggered by a low -raft-snap threshold, or right after a file is created but possibly before its sidecar is written.
promises.outside_observation: After restart, either the node serves /readyz and returns every acknowledged write, or it exits and logs a CRC or integrity error. Fuss can read each data file and its sidecar, recompute the CRC itself, and check that refusal happens only when the CRCs differ. The key bug signal is a node that starts and serves data even though Fuss's recomputed CRC mismatches the sidecar. A second signal is a node that refuses to start after an ordinary crash with no external modification. That is not a broken promise, but it is a false positive worth reporting.
promises.workload_sketch: Start rqlited with -raft-snap=50 and a data dir. Loop POST /db/execute 'INSERT INTO t(v) VALUES(?)' with unique values, recording each acknowledgement. SIGKILL at a random moment. Snapshot the data dir read-only and recompute CRCs against the sidecars. Restart with the same flags. Record whether the process exits or becomes ready. If ready, GET /db/query?level=strong 'SELECT v FROM t' and compare the result to the acknowledged writes.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: if the data file and its sidecar are not written and fsynced as a unit, a crash between them could leave a stale sidecar. That would make a healthy node refuse to start, or leave a file with no sidecar that gets skipped and never checked.

promises.quote: The node refuses to run if any file fails the check. This catches bitrot, or other modification, that may have occurred while a node is shut down.
promises.plain: Data files left truncated or incomplete by running out of disk must be caught at the next startup instead of being silently used.
promises.when_to_inject: Fill the filesystem holding the data dir while writes and snapshots are in progress. Then stop the node and free the space before restarting.
promises.outside_observation: On restart, either startup is clean and every acknowledged write is present, or the node refuses to start with an integrity error. Fuss can recompute CRCs over the files and compare them to the sidecars to confirm that rqlite's decision matches. A bug is a node that starts while serving fewer rows than were acknowledged, or that returns 'malformed' errors.
promises.workload_sketch: Mount a small tmpfs or loop filesystem as the data dir. Start rqlited with -raft-snap=50. Insert rows until the disk fills, recording acknowledgements and errors. Kill the node, enlarge or free the filesystem, and restart. Check /readyz, then GET /db/query?level=strong 'SELECT count(*), max(v) FROM t' against the acknowledged set.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a short write under ENOSPC might be computed or recorded in the sidecar inconsistently, or an error path might leave a partial snapshot file that the next startup treats as valid.

promises.quote: When a Leader sends a snapshot to a Follower, it sends the stored CRC with it. The Follower recomputes the CRC over the bytes it received and rejects the snapshot if the values do not match.
promises.plain: A follower never installs a snapshot whose received bytes fail the CRC, so a cut-off or damaged transfer never becomes the follower's state.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the leader, or the follower, while the leader is streaming a snapshot to a lagging or new follower. A large dataset makes the transfer window wide enough to hit.
promises.outside_observation: Once the cluster has healed, the follower either completes catch-up and returns exactly the leader's rows, or it keeps retrying. It must never serve a partial dataset. Fuss compares GET /db/query?level=none on the follower with ?level=strong on the leader, and also checks that every snapshot file in the follower's data dir has a sidecar CRC that matches Fuss's own recomputation.
promises.workload_sketch: Start a 3-node cluster with -raft-snap=100. Stop node3. Insert about 200k rows on the leader so it snapshots and truncates its log. Restart node3 so it needs a snapshot install. During the transfer, SIGKILL the leader or node3. Restart all nodes. Poll node3 until it is ready, then compare SELECT count(*), sum(v) on node3 (level=none) with the leader (level=strong).
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: if the follower checks the CRC only after it has partly applied or renamed the incoming snapshot, a crash in that window could leave half-installed state that is used on restart.

promises.quote: After rqlite merges previously snapshotted SQLite data, it runs SQLite's [`PRAGMA quick_check`](https://sqlite.org/pragma.html#pragma_quick_check) against the resulting database. The check walks most of the database's internal structure: B-trees and page references. A failure causes rqlite to log the error and refuse to proceed with the new state.
promises.plain: A database whose structure is broken after a snapshot merge is never served. rqlite logs an error and refuses it instead.
promises.when_to_inject: SIGKILL during frequent snapshotting, when previously snapshotted data is being merged, or during the restart that follows such a crash.
promises.outside_observation: After restart, the node either refuses to proceed and logs a quick_check failure, or it serves queries cleanly. Fuss runs GET /db/query 'PRAGMA integrity_check' and full-table scans. Any 'database disk image is malformed' error, or any row count below the acknowledged writes, while the node reports itself ready means the promise is broken.
promises.workload_sketch: Start a single node with -raft-snap=20 -raft-snap-int=1s. Run continuous INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE operations with an index on column v. SIGKILL at random intervals, then restart. After each restart, check /readyz, then query 'PRAGMA integrity_check', 'SELECT count(*) FROM t', and 'SELECT * FROM t ORDER BY v' against Fuss's model.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the check might run only on one merge path, such as snapshot install, and not on the crash-recovery merge at startup, so damaged state could slip through there.

promises.quote: When a node detects corruption -- at startup, on snapshot receive, or during `PRAGMA quick_check` -- it refuses to use the bad data.
promises.plain: Whenever corruption is detected, the node does not serve or replicate the bad data.
promises.when_to_inject: Restart the node after any crash or disk-full episode in which Fuss's own CRC recomputation shows a mismatch between a data file and its sidecar.
promises.outside_observation: If Fuss's recomputed CRC mismatches the sidecar, the node must not become ready, must not answer queries with data, and must not hand that data to peers. Fuss checks that /readyz never succeeds and that other nodes' contents still match Fuss's acknowledged history.
promises.workload_sketch: Reuse the crash and disk-full loops above. Whenever a pre-restart CRC scan finds a mismatch, restart the node and poll /readyz and GET /db/query on it for 60 seconds. Query the healthy peers with level=strong and compare their results to the model.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a node might refuse locally yet still take part in Raft (for example by voting) or serve level=none reads before the check finishes.

promises.quote: To recover, ensure the node is stopped, remove its data directory, restart it, and let it rejoin the cluster. Alternatively remove and deprovision the node, and add a new node to the cluster. In either case rqlite will replicate the current state from the Leader.
promises.plain: A node restarted with an empty data directory rejoins the cluster and ends up with exactly the leader's current state.
promises.when_to_inject: Stop a follower and restart it with the same -node-id but a fresh, empty data directory path (Fuss never writes to the old directory). Optionally SIGKILL the leader while the fresh node is catching up.
promises.outside_observation: The fresh node eventually reports ready and its full dataset (level=none) equals the leader's (level=strong) and Fuss's acknowledged history. No acknowledged write is missing and no unacknowledged-then-rolled-back write appears.
promises.workload_sketch: Start a 3-node cluster. Run continuous inserts with unique ids, logging acknowledgements to a Fuss history file. Stop node2 and restart it with -node-id=node2, a new empty data dir, and -join pointing at a live peer. While it catches up, keep writing and optionally SIGKILL and restart the leader. Once all nodes are ready, compare SELECT id FROM t ORDER BY id on node2 (level=none, after a brief settle) and on the leader (level=strong) against the history.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a node rejoining with the same ID but no state could be confused with its old Raft identity, especially across a leader change mid-catch-up, and end up stuck or missing log entries applied before its snapshot.

promises.quote: This path depends on the cluster having quorum and at least one healthy peer with intact data.
promises.plain: Recovery by re-replication works only while a quorum and a healthy peer exist. Without quorum, the wiped node must not invent or serve state of its own.
promises.when_to_inject: SIGKILL enough nodes to lose quorum, then start a follower with a fresh, empty data directory.
promises.outside_observation: The fresh node does not become ready and does not accept writes or serve an empty dataset as authoritative. Once quorum is restored, it catches up to the full acknowledged history.
promises.workload_sketch: Start a 3-node cluster and insert N rows, recording acknowledgements. SIGKILL node1 and node3. Start node2 with a fresh data dir and -join pointing at the dead peers. Send POST /db/execute and GET /db/query?level=strong to node2 and expect errors or timeouts. Restart node1 and node3, then verify that node2 converges to N rows.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a fresh node with a wiped data dir might bootstrap itself as a new single-node cluster if the join fails, splitting off with empty state.
